slots.practicalActivity: Draw a data-flow diagram for Northbridge Retail's checkout flow (customer browser, checkout service, payment processor, order database, inventory service), mark every trust boundary with a dashed line, then run STRIDE against each boundary-crossing arrow — writing one concrete, defensible threat per category (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) — and note which later-course control would catch each threat earliest.
slots.deliverable: A diagrammed checkout data-flow diagram with trust boundaries marked, plus a six-row STRIDE table with one real threat and its earliest-catch control per category.

lessons.title: The OWASP Top 10 for DevOps Teams

slots.practicalActivity: Walk Northbridge Retail's checkout service through all seven SSDLC stages (Plan, Design, Develop, Build/Test, Release, Deploy, Operate/Maintain), writing one concrete security activity for each stage, then tag each activity with the OWASP Top 10 category it's primarily designed to catch (e.g. an IaC scan at Build/Test maps to Security Misconfiguration; audit logging at Operate maps to Security Logging and Alerting Failures).
slots.deliverable: A written seven-row SSDLC table for the checkout service, each row naming a concrete security activity and its matching OWASP Top 10 category.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review: pick a second Northbridge Retail service you haven't modeled yet (e.g. the inventory service), build its own data-flow diagram and STRIDE threat table from scratch without referencing the checkout example, then write a short comparison of which trust boundaries and threat categories recur versus which are unique to this service.
slots.deliverable: An independently built data-flow diagram and STRIDE table for a second Northbridge Retail service, plus a written comparison against the checkout example.

slots.practicalActivity: Using a free-tier or trial Azure subscription, open a resource group's Access control (IAM) blade and create a least-privilege role assignment for a fictional 'Checkout Service Operator' (Reader scoped to just that resource group, not the subscription), then read it back the way an auditor would — name the exact security principal, role definition, and scope — and write down why a subscription-level Contributor grant for the same task would violate least privilege.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure role assignment scoped to one resource group, plus a written who/what/where audit breakdown and an explanation of why a broader scope would violate least privilege.

slots.practicalActivity: Write an IAM permissions policy JSON granting only `s3:GetObject` on one specific bucket ARN (never `s3:*` / `Resource: *`), attach it to a role with a trust policy limited to the EC2 service, and if you have an AWS sandbox, create the role and use the IAM policy simulator (or `aws iam simulate-principal-policy`) to confirm it's allowed on that one bucket and denied on every other action and resource.
slots.deliverable: A least-privilege IAM role (trust policy + permissions policy) scoped to one S3 bucket's ARN, plus policy-simulator output confirming the allow/deny boundary.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a namespaced Role granting only get/list/watch on pods in a `checkout` namespace, bind it to a ServiceAccount with a RoleBinding, and verify least privilege with `kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:checkout:checkout-monitor` (should allow) versus the same check against secrets (should deny); then write the Azure AD Workload Identity federation definition that would bind that same ServiceAccount to an Entra ID application holding only the Key Vault Secrets User role on one vault, with no client secret stored anywhere.
slots.deliverable: A Role+RoleBinding manifest with two `kubectl auth can-i` outputs (one allow, one deny), plus a workload-identity federation definition naming the exact single scoped role granted.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review: for one Northbridge Retail service of your choosing, write its complete identity chain end to end — its Azure RBAC role assignment, its Kubernetes Role+RoleBinding, and its workload identity federation to exactly one scoped cloud permission — annotating each layer with the one sentence that justifies why it isn't broader.
slots.deliverable: A written three-layer identity chain (Azure RBAC, Kubernetes RBAC, workload identity federation) for one service, each layer justified in one sentence.

slots.practicalActivity: List the four leak patterns (committed to source control, logged in plaintext, baked into an image, shared out of band) and write a one-line Northbridge Retail example of each happening to a payment API key; then create a real secret in Azure Key Vault (or a trial vault), confirm its value is hidden behind 'Show Secret Value,' update it once to see Key Vault auto-version it, and grant yourself a Key Vault Secrets User role scoped to just that vault to read it back.
slots.deliverable: A written list mapping all four leak patterns to a concrete payment-key scenario, plus a real Key Vault secret with at least two versions and a scoped Key Vault Secrets User role reading it back.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a secret in AWS Secrets Manager (console or `aws secretsmanager create-secret`) structured as JSON key/value pairs for a fake database credential, configure (or fully document, if no RDS instance is available) a managed rotation schedule, and write the least-privilege IAM policy restricting `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` to that one secret's exact ARN, including its random suffix.
slots.deliverable: A real (or fully specified) Secrets Manager secret with a rotation configuration, plus an IAM policy scoped to that one secret's exact ARN.

slots.practicalActivity: Run Vault in dev mode locally (`vault server -dev`), enable a new KV version-2 secrets engine at a custom mount path, write and read back a secret through the CLI, then write out how Vault's database secrets engine would issue Northbridge Retail's checkout service a brand-new, short-lived database credential per request instead of one long-lived password to rotate.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of a local Vault dev server with a custom-path KV v2 engine holding a real written-and-read secret, plus a written explanation of dynamic database credentials replacing one long-lived password.

slots.practicalActivity: Decode a sample base64 Kubernetes Secret value by hand (`echo <value> | base64 -d`) to prove it isn't encryption, write an ExternalSecret manifest syncing a Key Vault/Vault secret into a native Kubernetes Secret, and write a GitHub Actions workflow step referencing `secrets.DB_PASSWORD` through the `secrets` context to confirm it never appears literally in the workflow file.
slots.deliverable: A terminal decode proving base64 isn't encryption, an ExternalSecret manifest, and a GitHub Actions workflow snippet correctly referencing a secret through the `secrets` context.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review: trace one fictional secret (a shipping-carrier API key) from its real home in Key Vault, through an ExternalSecret sync into a Kubernetes Secret, into a pod's environment variable, and into a GitHub Actions deploy step — naming the specific control at each hop (RBAC, sync interval, log masking) that keeps it from leaking there.
slots.deliverable: A written end-to-end trace of one secret's path from vault to running pod to pipeline, with the specific control named at each hop.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a small, deliberately vulnerable code snippet (e.g. a SQL query built by string concatenation from a request parameter), enable GitHub code scanning (CodeQL) on a real or sample repo, push it, confirm CodeQL flags it as a potential injection on the pull request check, then fix it with a parameterized query and confirm the alert clears.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub code scanning alert triggered by a deliberately vulnerable snippet, plus the pull request check showing the alert clear after the fix.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a deliberately outdated, known-vulnerable package version to a sample project's manifest (npm/pip), enable Dependabot alerts on the repo, confirm it surfaces the CVE with its CVSS severity and tags, use 'Create Dependabot security update' to generate the upgrade PR, and write one paragraph on whether this package would be reachable from a service's live request path if it were only a transitive dependency.
slots.deliverable: A real Dependabot alert for a deliberately vulnerable dependency plus the auto-generated upgrade pull request, and a written reachability note.

slots.practicalActivity: Commit a fake-but-realistic AWS access key into a sample repo, run gitleaks against it locally to see the real finding fields (RuleID, Entropy, File, Line, Fingerprint), delete the line in a follow-up commit and confirm with `git log -p` that the key is still recoverable from history, then 'rotate' it by replacing it with a real vault reference and note what push protection would have caught earlier.
slots.deliverable: A real gitleaks finding on a planted secret, proof via git history that deleting the line doesn't remove it, and a written note on push protection's earlier catch point.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a Terraform `azurerm_storage_account` resource with public network access left enabled, run Checkov against it locally or in CI, read the real finding fields (check ID, resource, file/line, guide link), then add the one line restricting public access and confirm the check passes on rerun — all before ever running `terraform apply`.
slots.deliverable: A before/after Checkov scan on one Terraform resource: a failed CKV_AZURE_59-style finding, the one-line fix, and a passing rerun, with apply never run against the vulnerable version.

lessons.title: Software Bills of Materials & Supply Chain Risk

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a real SBOM for a sample project with Syft (or Trivy's SBOM mode) in CycloneDX format, inspect the resulting JSON's `purl` entries, then simulate 'the morning after a new CVE' by picking one real component from your SBOM and writing the exact query you'd run across every stored SBOM to find every service using that package and version.
slots.deliverable: A real generated CycloneDX SBOM file plus a written query/search plan for answering 'are we affected' across multiple services' SBOMs.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a non-hardened Dockerfile (`FROM ubuntu:22.04`, root user, single stage) for a trivial app, scan it with Trivy and record the CRITICAL/HIGH counts, then rewrite it as a hardened multi-stage build (distroless or `-slim` final stage, non-root `USER`, no shell) and rescan to show the finding count drop.
slots.deliverable: Two Trivy scan outputs — before and after hardening the same Dockerfile — showing a measurable drop in CRITICAL/HIGH findings.

slots.practicalActivity: Label a namespace `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`, attempt to apply a Pod spec that runs as root/privileged and confirm Kubernetes rejects it, then fix the spec with the exact `securityContext` fields (`runAsNonRoot`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`) and confirm it's admitted into the same restricted namespace.
slots.deliverable: Terminal proof of a Pod Security Standards rejection for a non-compliant spec, followed by a corrected spec with the four securityContext fields successfully admitted.

slots.practicalActivity: In a real GitHub repo, create a `production` Environment under Settings → Environments, add yourself as a required reviewer, wire a deploy job to target that environment, trigger it and confirm it pauses on a pending deployment, approve it, then locate the 'Start all waiting jobs' bypass control and write down why a visible, logged bypass is still an acceptable control while a silent one wouldn't be.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub Environment with a required reviewer that paused and was approved, plus a written note on why a visible bypass preserves the control's integrity.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Falco on a test cluster or VM (or carefully review its documented install), deploy the `shell_in_container` rule exactly as written, exec a shell into a running container to deliberately trigger it, and confirm the alert fires with the correct `%user.name`/`%container.name` fields populated; then write why this event is especially alarming on a distroless image like the hardened checkout build from the Image Scanning lesson.
slots.deliverable: A real Falco alert triggered by a deliberate exec-into-container shell, with a written explanation of why it's a stronger signal on a distroless image.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Gatekeeper on a test cluster, deploy the `K8sRequiredLabels` ConstraintTemplate and a Constraint requiring a `cost-center` label on every Namespace exactly as shown, attempt to create a namespace without that label and confirm Gatekeeper's admission controller rejects it, then add the label and confirm it's admitted.
slots.deliverable: A real Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate + Constraint pair with terminal proof of both a rejected and an admitted Namespace creation based on a required label.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a Chef InSpec control mapping PCI-DSS Requirement 3 to a disk/database-encryption check for a fictional `nb-payments-db` resource, then open a real or sandbox Azure resource's Activity Log, identify an entry showing which identity performed an operation, and write the diagnostic-setting configuration that would forward that log to a Log Analytics workspace with 1-year retention to satisfy PCI-DSS Requirement 10.
slots.deliverable: An InSpec control mapped to PCI-DSS Req 3, a real/example Activity Log entry identifying the acting identity, and a diagnostic-setting configuration meeting a 1-year retention requirement.

slots.practicalActivity: Take 3-5 real or sample scanner findings (mixed severities/sources — e.g. one from your Trivy image scan, one from your Dependabot alert), run each through all five stages (triage, prioritize, remediate, verify, report) with a short note per stage per finding, and rank them using both CVSS score and exploitability/business context — not CVSS alone — explaining any case where that second factor changes the ranking.
slots.deliverable: A five-stage vulnerability-management log for 3-5 real findings, with a written ranking showing at least one case where exploitability/context reordered a pure CVSS ranking.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a tabletop incident scenario for Northbridge Retail (a leaked payment-API key or anomalous database read pattern) and walk it through all four NIST SP 800-61 phases in writing — Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity — ending with at least two concrete changes that feed back into Preparation.
slots.deliverable: A written tabletop incident walkthrough covering all four NIST SP 800-61 phases with at least two concrete post-incident changes.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Secure a Pipeline End to End

slots.practicalActivity: Write the capstone's acceptance checklist for securing Northbridge Retail's order-service pipeline: name all six required controls (secrets scan, SAST, dependency scan, image scan, policy gate, least-privilege deploy identity) in order, and draft one realistic sample finding each scanner would catch (a hardcoded key, a SQL-injection pattern, a vulnerable package, a CRITICAL base-image CVE).
slots.deliverable: A written acceptance checklist naming all six controls in order plus one realistic sample finding per scanner.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the six-stage pipeline definition (as YAML/pseudocode or a real CI config) in the exact order from the lesson — secrets-scan → SAST → dependency-scan → build → image-scan → policy-gate → deploy — write a precise, implementable policy-gate rule (block on any secrets match, or CVSS ≥9.0 SAST/dependency finding, or an unexcluded critical image finding), and define order-service's least-privilege deploy identity naming exactly the Key Vault secrets, log targets, and deploy scope it needs and nothing else.
slots.deliverable: A complete pipeline-stage definition in the correct order, a precise policy-gate rule, and an explicit least-privilege identity permission list for order-service.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement the capstone pipeline for real against a sample order-service (or reuse product-catalog/checkout from the DevOps Capstone course) in GitHub Actions — wire real tools to each stage (gitleaks for secrets, a SAST tool like Semgrep or CodeQL, Trivy/npm-audit for dependencies, Trivy for the image) — then trigger the pipeline against a deliberately planted secret and a deliberately vulnerable dependency and confirm the policy gate actually blocks deploy on both.
slots.deliverable: A real, running GitHub Actions pipeline implementing all six controls, with two captured runs proving the policy gate blocks a planted secret and a vulnerable dependency.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the three-question retrospective format from the Security Incident Response lesson on your own capstone build (what happened, what worked, what would you change), then write and rehearse the four-part presentation structure (the problem, the design, one concrete trade-off, what you'd do with more time) you'd give in a portfolio writeup or technical interview.
slots.deliverable: A written retrospective plus a rehearsed four-part presentation script for the order-service capstone pipeline.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can threat-model a real service with STRIDE, implement least-privilege identity across Azure, AWS, and Kubernetes, manage secrets through a real vault instead of plaintext, wire SAST, dependency, secrets, IaC, and image scanning plus policy-as-code gates into a CI/CD pipeline, and run a security incident through the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle — proven by building and presenting a six-control secured pipeline for Northbridge Retail's order-service.
